subject: Physics
text: In a region, the electric potential varies as V = 10 − 50x, where V is in volts and x in metres. The electric field in the region is (2026 Board)
explanation: E = −dV/dx = −50 ×(−50)... actually dV/dx = −50, so E = −(dV/dx) = 50 N/C, directed along +x (since V decreases as x increases).
whyWrong: Magnitude is 50 N/C not 10 N/C; dV/dx = −50, not −10.
Magnitude is wrong and direction is also wrong.
Correct: E = −dV/dx = 50 N/C along +x.
Direction is wrong; since V decreases with increasing x, E points along +x, not −x.

subject: Physics
text: A conducting wire connects two charged metallic spheres A and B of radii r1 and r2 respectively (distance between them very large compared to radii). The ratio of electric fields (E_A/E_B) at the surfaces of the spheres will be (2026 Board)
explanation: Connected spheres reach the same potential V. Since V = kQ/r, surface field E = V/r. So E_A/E_B = (V/r1)/(V/r2) = r2/r1.
whyWrong: This is the inverse ratio.
Correct: E_A/E_B = r2/r1 since surface field is V/r at common potential V.
This uses a squared dependence that doesn't apply to E = V/r.
This is the inverse of the squared ratio; also the wrong power.

subject: Physics
text: A long straight wire of circular cross-section (radius a) carries a steady current I, uniformly distributed across the cross-section. The magnitude of the magnetic field at a point at distance a/2 from the axis of the wire is (2026 Board)
explanation: Inside a uniformly current-carrying wire, B = μ₀Ir/(2πa²). At r = a/2, B = μ₀I(a/2)/(2πa²) = μ₀I/(4πa).
whyWrong: Field is not zero inside a current-carrying wire away from the axis.
This is the field value at the surface (r = a), not at r = a/2.
Correct: substituting r = a/2 into B = μ₀Ir/(2πa²) gives μ₀I/(4πa).
This does not match the inside-wire formula evaluated at r = a/2.

subject: Physics
text: The shape of the interference fringes in Young's double-slit experiment, when the distance between the slit and the screen is very large compared to the slit separation, is nearly (2026 Board)
explanation: When D >> d, the hyperbolic fringes (loci of constant path difference) become nearly straight lines parallel to the slits.
whyWrong: Correct: for D >> d the hyperbolas flatten into nearly straight lines.
Fringes are not parabolic in this geometry.
Fringes are circular only very close to the slits, not far away.

subject: Physics
text: An electromagnetic wave passes from vacuum into a dielectric medium with relative electrical permittivity 3/2 and relative magnetic permeability 8/3. Then, its (2026 Board)
options: wavelength is doubled and frequency remains unchanged.
wavelength is doubled and frequency is halved.
wavelength is halved and frequency remains unchanged.
wavelength and frequency both remain unchanged.
explanation: Refractive index n = √(εrμr) = √(3/2 × 8/3) = √4 = 2. Frequency is set by the source and doesn't change; speed becomes v = c/n = c/2, so wavelength λ = v/f is halved.
whyWrong: Wavelength decreases, it does not double.
Wavelength decreases (not doubles) and frequency never changes at a boundary.
Correct: n = 2, so speed and hence wavelength halve while frequency (set by source) is unchanged.
Wavelength does change since the medium's refractive index is 2, not 1.

subject: Physics
text: In a series LCR circuit, the voltage across the resistor, capacitor and inductor is 10 V each. If the capacitor is short-circuited, the voltage across the inductor will be (2026 Board)
explanation: Originally VL = VC so the circuit is at resonance and source voltage = VR = 10 V, with XL = XC = VL/I = R. Shorting C leaves R and L in series with the same source (10 V). New impedance Z' = √(R²+XL²) = R√2 (since XL=R), so new current I' = I/√2, and new VL' = I'XL = (I/√2)·R = 10/√2 = 5√2/... recomputing: VL' = I'·XL = (10/(R√2)) · R = 10/√2 = 5√2 V.
whyWrong: This ignores the change in circuit impedance after removing C.
This ignores the factor of √2 in the new impedance.
Correct: VL' = 10/√2 = 5√2 V after the capacitor is shorted.
This is too large; the new inductor voltage decreases relative to 10√2, not increases.

subject: Physics
text: Electromagnetic waves used as a diagnostic tool in medicine (X-rays) have a wavelength range (2026 Board)
explanation: X-rays, used in medical imaging, have wavelengths roughly from about 1 nm down to 10⁻³ nm (or even shorter), much shorter than visible or infrared light.
whyWrong: Correct: this is the X-ray wavelength range used in diagnostic imaging.
This range (400 nm–1 nm) spans visible/UV, not the X-ray diagnostic range.

subject: Physics
text: The 'distance of closest approach' of an alpha particle is 'd' when it moves with velocity v head-on towards the target nucleus. If the velocity of the alpha particle is halved, the new distance of closest approach will be (2026 Board)
explanation: At closest approach, all KE converts to electrostatic PE: (1/2)mv² = kZe(2e)/d, so d ∝ 1/v². Halving v makes d increase by a factor of 4.
whyWrong: This suggests d decreases, but d must increase as v decreases.
This is only a factor of 2, but d ∝ 1/v² gives a factor of 4.
Correct: since d ∝ 1/v², halving v quadruples d.
d increases, it does not decrease.

subject: Physics
text: A concave lens of focal length 10 cm is cut into two identical plano-concave lenses. The focal length of each lens will be (2026 Board)
explanation: Cutting a symmetric biconcave lens along its axis into two plano-concave halves keeps each curved-surface radius the same but removes one curved surface, halving the lens power (1/f ∝ sum of curvatures), so each half has double the focal length: 2 × 10 cm = 20 cm.
whyWrong: Correct: each half has double the original focal length.
This is triple the focal length, not double.
This is quadruple, not double, the original focal length.
This would mean the power increased, but cutting a lens this way reduces power, increasing focal length.

subject: Physics
text: Four independent waves are y1=A1 sinωt, y2=A2 sin2ωt, y3=A3 cosωt, y4=A4 sin(ωt+π/3). Interference between two of these waves is possible in (2026 Board)
explanation: Sustained interference requires the same frequency (and a constant phase difference). y1, y3 and y4 all have angular frequency ω; y2 has frequency 2ω and cannot sustain interference with the others.
whyWrong: This excludes y4, which also has frequency ω and can interfere with y1 and y3.
This excludes y1, which also shares frequency ω.
Correct: y1, y3, y4 share frequency ω and can mutually interfere; y2 has a different frequency.
y2 has frequency 2ω, different from the others, so it cannot show sustained interference with them.

text: In an unbiased p-n junction, at equilibrium, which of the following statements is true? (2026 Board)
options: Diffusion current is zero but drift current exists.
Diffusion current exists but drift current is zero.
Diffusion and drift currents are equal and opposite.
Both diffusion and drift currents exist but are unequal.
explanation: At equilibrium (no external bias), the diffusion current (majority carriers moving across the junction) is exactly balanced by the drift current (minority carriers swept by the built-in field), giving zero net current.
whyWrong: Both currents exist at equilibrium, not just drift.
Both currents exist at equilibrium, not just diffusion.
Correct: at equilibrium the two currents are equal and opposite, giving zero net current.
They are equal (not unequal); that's precisely why net current is zero at equilibrium.

subject: Physics
text: Assertion (A): All atoms have a net magnetic moment. Reason (R): A current loop does not always behave as a magnetic dipole. (2026 Board)
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are false.
explanation: A is false: atoms with fully filled subshells (e.g. noble gases) have zero net magnetic moment due to paired electron spins/orbital motions cancelling. R is also false: a current loop always behaves as a magnetic dipole, with moment m = IA.
whyWrong: A is false (not all atoms have a net moment), so this cannot be correct regardless of R.
Neither statement is true.
R is also false, not merely a poor explanation-mismatch case.
Correct: neither statement is true – many atoms have zero net moment, and a current loop always behaves as a magnetic dipole.

text: Assertion (A): If accelerated electrons are passed through a narrow slit, a diffraction pattern is observed. Reason (R): Electrons behave as both particles and waves. (2026 Board)

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

explanation: Electrons indeed produce diffraction patterns (as in the Davisson-Germer experiment), confirming their wave nature. This is precisely because electrons exhibit wave-particle duality, which is the correct explanation.
whyWrong: This under-credits R, which is exactly why diffraction is observed.
R does directly explain A, not merely accompany it.
R is true, not false – wave-particle duality is well established for electrons.
Correct: diffraction of electrons is direct evidence of their wave nature, correctly explained by wave-particle duality.

subject: Physics
text: Assertion (A): The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of the constituent nucleons. Reason (R): Energy is absorbed when the nucleons are bound together to form a nucleus. (2026 Board)
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are false.
explanation: A is true: this mass difference is the mass defect, converted to binding energy. But R is false: energy is released (not absorbed) when nucleons bind together, which is why the bound nucleus has less mass (E=Δmc² is released).
whyWrong: R is false; energy is released, not absorbed, during nucleon binding.
R is false outright, not merely a non-explanation.
Correct: mass defect (A) is true, but binding releases energy rather than absorbing it, so R is false.
A is definitely true – nuclear mass is always less than the sum of nucleon masses.

subject: Physics
text: Assertion (A): In Bohr model of hydrogen atom, the energy levels are discrete and quantised. Reason (R): In a hydrogen atom, the electrostatic force on the electron provides the necessary centripetal force to it to revolve around the nucleus. (2026 Board)
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are false.
explanation: Both statements are true: energy levels are indeed quantised, and Coulomb attraction does supply centripetal force. But R alone (classical circular motion) doesn't explain quantisation – that requires Bohr's separate postulate on angular momentum quantisation (L = nh/2π).
whyWrong: R by itself does not explain why energy levels are discrete; that requires the separate angular-momentum quantisation postulate.
Correct: both are true, but the centripetal-force condition alone doesn't explain quantisation of energy levels.
R is true, not false – Coulomb force does provide the centripetal force in the Bohr model.
Both statements are true, not false.

text: Three point charges 2q, −2q and q are kept at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side l. The potential energy of the system is (2026 Board)
explanation: U = k[(2q)(−2q) + (2q)(q) + (−2q)(q)]/l = k(−4q²+2q²−2q²)/l = −4kq²/l = −q²/(πε₀l) using k=1/(4πε₀).
whyWrong: The pairwise energies don't cancel to zero; the net sum is −4kq²/l.
This has the wrong coefficient.
This has the wrong sign and coefficient.

text: Two metal spheres of radii r1 and r2 (>r1) having charges q1 and q2 respectively kept in air, are brought in contact. Which statement is NOT correct? (2026 Board)

explanation: r_n ∝ n², so Δr = r_{n+1} − r_n ≈ dr/dn = (const)×2n ∝ n for large n.

text: A galvanometer of resistance 27 Ω is converted into an ammeter of range (0–10 mA) using a shunt resistance of 3 Ω. The galvanometer will show full-scale deflection for a current of about (2026 Board)
explanation: For a shunt, Ig×G = (I−Ig)×S. With G=27, S=3, I=10 mA: Ig×27 = (10−Ig)×3 → 27Ig = 30−3Ig → 30Ig=30 → Ig=1 mA.
whyWrong: 10 mA is the full ammeter range, not the galvanometer's own full-scale current.
This is far too large for the galvanometer's small share of current.

text: The magnetic flux ϕ (in Wb) linked with a coil is related to time t (in s) as ϕ = 5At² + Bt − 2C. The SI units of A and B are respectively (2026 Board)

subject: Physics
text: A magnet held vertically, with its north pole down, is dropped along the axis of a closed solenoid placed vertically on a table. Looking down from the top, (2026 Board)
options: the induced current will flow anticlockwise.
the induced current will flow clockwise.
no induced current will flow in the solenoid.
the magnet will fall with a constant velocity.
explanation: As the N-pole approaches from above, flux into the top of the solenoid increases; by Lenz's law the induced current opposes this by creating a N-pole facing upward at the top, which (by the right-hand rule, viewed from above) requires anticlockwise current.
whyWrong: Correct: to oppose the increasing downward-into-the-solenoid flux, the top face must become a north pole, requiring anticlockwise current viewed from above.
This direction would create a south pole facing the approaching magnet, which would attract rather than oppose it – violating Lenz's law.
A changing flux is definitely induced as the magnet falls through, so current does flow.
The magnet accelerates under gravity (opposed partly by the induced eddy effect), it does not fall at constant velocity in a simple closed solenoid loop.

text: Assertion (A): Two electric heaters of power P1 and P2 (>P1) are joined in series across a dc source of voltage V.
